solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

E045-01.notes: Comma + 'and' correctly joins two independent clauses ('Some of them remembered...' / 'they wanted...'). B: comma splice. C: comma after the conjunction 'and' is wrong. D: comma separates subject 'they' from verb 'wanted'.

E045-02.notes: Paired commas set off the nonrestrictive clause 'whose small company, Nordic Ware, made kitchen products from cast aluminum' between subject 'Dalquist' and verb 'agreed'. B: drops the opening comma, leaving an unbalanced clause. C: semicolon leaves 'Dalquist' as a fragment. D: 'his small company' makes the company an appositive to Dalquist, and 'Nordic Ware, made... agreed to try' then has two verbs with no grammatical link; meaning breaks too.

E045-03.notes: Concise. B: 'made it possible... to be able to' is redundant and wordy. C: 'let... be able to' is redundant. D: 'allowed and permitted' is redundant.

flags.note: 'Slow' is a recognized flat adverb in informal usage ('go slow'), but in ACT-standard written English 'slowly' is clearly the best answer; no real second answer.

E045-04.notes: Adverb needed to modify the verb 'sold'. A: adjective 'slow' in place of the adverb (informal). C/D: comparative forms with nothing to compare to; D is also a nonstandard comparative.

E045-05.notes: The aluminum facts (most abundant metal in the crust; aircraft, cans) are accurate but off-topic for a paragraph about designing and naming the pan. A: the sentence says nothing about weight or why Dalquist chose aluminum. B: the pan's strength isn't the paragraph's point, and the sentence doesn't say that. D: nothing in it contradicts 'lighter'.

E045-06.notes: Sentence 7 gives the cause of the slow sales, so 'One reason was that' fits. B: reverses the cause and effect (shoppers' unfamiliarity was not caused by slow sales). C/D: contrast transitions where no contrast exists.

flags.note: In A, someone could argue the fudge ring was also 'baked in a Bundt pan', but the modifier logically describes the cake, and D is clearly best. Minor factual nuance: the fudge 'tunnel' comes from the gooey, underset center created during baking; 'as it cooled' is a simplification but acceptable.

E045-07.notes: The opening modifier must describe the cake, so the subject has to be 'her "Tunnel of Fudge" cake' (D). A: dangling, with 'a ring of soft fudge' as subject and an unclear 'it'. B: says Helfrich was baked in a Bundt pan. C: the expletive 'there was' leaves the modifier with no subject to attach to; wordy.

E045-08.notes: Singular possessive: one contest owns the 'best-known entry'. A: plural with no apostrophe. B: plural possessive, but there is only one contest. D: no possessive; 'the contest best-known entry' is ungrammatical.

E045-09.notes: The subject is the singular 'flood' (with 'of requests from bakers who wanted...' coming between subject and verb), so the verb is 'was', in past tense to match 'had to expand'. A/C/D: plural verbs ('were', 'are', 'have been'); C and D also shift the tense.

E045-10.notes: The essay traces a decade of slow sales, then a surge after the 1966 Bake-Off entry. A: the design details are a small part and don't address the goal. C: the club members appear only at the opening. D: false, because the essay states the cake 'won second place'.
